title: "Dukha"
subtitle: "Mongolia"
region: "East Asia"
tags: [ethnography, east-asia]

## Overview

The Dukha, also called Duha, Dukhans, Duhalar, or Tsaatan, are a small Turkic community of semi-nomadic reindeer herders living in Tsagaannuur sum of Khövsgöl Province, northern Mongolia. They are divided into East Taiga and West Taiga territorial groups, whose ancestral territories extended from northeast and southeast Tuva toward Lake Hövsgöl and Ulaan Taiga. The Dukha are Mongolia’s only reindeer herders, and their community is organized around domesticated reindeer, which provide milk, transportation, and materials for clothing and household objects. In 2000, 30–32 households, about 180 people, remained in Tsagaanuur with their reindeer, while the nomadic and settled Dukha populations together numbered about 500. Their endangered language belongs to the Taiga subgroup of Sayan Turkic.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

Dukha clothing includes hats like those of the Khalkh people and wide *deels*, traditional Mongolian overcoats. They wear strong, warm boots made from reindeer hides and sinew. Reindeer pelts are used for winter coats, while reindeer skin is used for bags, traveling mats, and shoes. The sources do not distinguish men’s and women’s everyday clothing, identify ceremonial dress, or describe belts, decorative techniques, or named clothing patterns. Only a few reindeer are slaughtered during the year for meat and pelts.

### Architecture

The Dukha live in *ortz*, yurts that resemble Native-American tepees. A large yurt may require birch bark from up to 32 trees, while a medium-sized yurt is made from the bark of 23–25 trees. Dukha communities on the taiga generally consist of tents belonging to two to seven households. Families belonging to the same residential group establish their tents close to one another, within a few kilometers, and cooperate in livestock herding. A residential group composed of several families is called *olal-lal* in the Tuva language.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Reindeer provide materials for several everyday objects: bags, traveling mats, shoes, winter coats, tools, souvenirs, saddles, and carts. Men make and repair hunting tools and reindeer saddles and carts. Reindeer antlers have been sold for decades for traditional Chinese medicine and are also carved into tools and used as souvenir material. The antlers are harvested annually in early summer, although this practice has begun to decline because of ethical concerns.

## Music & performance

They do describe shamanistic practices and ceremonies. Dukha shaman worship includes reverence for a shaman called *Boo*, as well as the use of mystical holy books and treatises in daily life. These texts include materials concerned with hunting and with calling or banishing the rain. Shaman ceremonies are held for welcoming the new moon, and specific practices are associated with retrieving river water.

## Festivals & rituals

They describe shaman ceremonies welcoming the new moon and practices connected with retrieving river water. Dukha religious traditions center on the sacredness of reindeer. This belief generally prevents the slaughter and eating of reindeer, which are treated with respect and, in many ways, as members of the household.

The Dukha believe in Shamanism, tengrism, and animism. Nature—including the earth and sky—and ancestors are revered as powerful forces governing human lives. During Communist rule in Mongolia from 1924–1992, these traditions were suppressed: shamans were arrested and ancestral tombs were smashed. After the end of Communist rule, the Dukha were again allowed to practice their traditional faith freely.

## Foodways

Reindeer milk, reindeer yoghurt, reindeer cheese, and milk tea are staples of the Dukha diet. The Dukha primarily raise reindeer for milk, and girls and younger women milk the animals and make yoghurt, cheese, and milk tea. Because reindeer are rarely killed, the Dukha supplement these products by hunting wild animals in the forest. The sources name elk, moose, bear, sable, and boar as hunted animals eaten for protein.

Reindeer also support mobility and subsistence: they transport people during daily grazing, hunting, firewood collection, seasonal migrations, visits, shopping, and trade.

## Oral tradition & literature

They state that the Dukha use mystical holy books and different treatises in daily life, including texts for hunting and for calling or banishing the rain.

Several organizations are described as supporting Dukha cultural continuity. The Totem Peoples Preservation Project and the Mongolian Reindeer Fund work to train herders and help preserve the health of their reindeer.

## Language & religion

Dukhan, also called Dukha, is an endangered or nearly extinct Turkic language or dialect variety of Tuvan. It belongs to the Taiga subgroup of Sayan Turkic and is closely related to Tuvan, Tofa, the language of Tozhu Tuvans, and Soyot. It is spoken in Tsagaan-Nuur County of Khövsgöl Province in northern Mongolia. The sources give approximately five hundred speakers in one account and no more than 40 active speakers in another. Today, many Dukha are fluent in Dukhan and Mongolian, while many young people are educated in Mongolia and are well-versed in Mongolian.

Dukha religion combines Shamanism, tengrism, and animism. The earth, sky, ancestors, and other aspects of nature are understood as powerful forces. Reindeer are sacred, and shamanistic practice includes reverence for *Boo*, mystical books, hunting treatises, rain-related practices, new-moon ceremonies, and river-water rituals.
